source.title: Overlooked Safety Vulnerability in LLMs: Malicious Intelligent Optimization Algorithm Request and its Jailbreak
source.authors: Hao-Ran Gu; Han-Ding Wang; Yi Mei; Meng-Jie Zhang; Yao-Chu Jin

page_placements.theme: Code, encodings and task reformulations bypass safeguards

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether a different jailbreak method—benign prompt rewriting—can increase harmful compliance in a new algorithm-design setting. It does not test the first-token mechanism or the other listed bypass methods.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates harmful compliance on original malicious algorithm-design prompts and prompts rewritten by MOBjailbreak. Only the rewritten-prompt results bear on V4; original-prompt results are recorded as related findings under fits_no_version. The input-token attention analysis in Figure 4 is not per-token KL across response positions and does not test V3 or the claimed explanation of shallowness.
record.test_reason: The study builds a benchmark of 60 malicious optimization-algorithm requests and tests MOBjailbreak, which uses a surrogate LLM to paraphrase each request into a benign-sounding one before sending it to the target. That is a prompt-level intent-masking attack. It is not prefilling a compliant response start, an adversarial suffix, or a decoding change. Nothing in it probes whether refusal sits in the first response tokens, so it does not measure what V4 names. There is no fine-tuning (V1, V2), no per-token KL (V3), no parameter localization (V5), no causal account of shallowness (V6), and no deepening defense (V7). The Figure 4 attention analysis scores input-token importance and does not cover response positions. Qi et al. (2310.03693) is cited only as the source of the 1–5 harmfulness rubric.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that current LLMs (mean ASR 83.59%) are vulnerable to malicious intelligent-optimization algorithm requests, and that MOBjailbreak's benign rewriting yields near-complete defense failure. They also find that plug-and-play defenses (SAGE, Self-Reminder) help on direct prompts but are only marginally effective against MOBjailbreak and can cause exaggerated safety. From the attention analysis, they argue models prioritize algorithm-design instructions over safety cues. They call for stronger alignment.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a benchmark of 60 malicious algorithm-design requests and a surrogate-LLM benign-rewriting jailbreak; it does not use fine-tuning or response-position KL measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by target model: standard-prompt ASR ranges from 38.33% to 100.00%, while MOBjailbreak ASR ranges from 88.33% to 100.00%. The paper also reports results under SAGE and Self-Reminder target/surrogate deployment settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Direct malicious algorithm-design requests get high compliance: 13-model mean ASR 83.59%, harm 4.28/5. GPT-5 (38.33%) and o3 (55.00%) are lowest; DeepSeek-V3/V3.1, Gemini, Doubao, Grok and ERNIE reach 100%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-trained LLMs often fail to refuse harmful requests framed as optimization-algorithm design, with large variation across models.

fits_no_version.finding: Surrogate-LLM benign paraphrasing (MOBjailbreak) raises mean ASR to 97.95% and harm to 4.87. The largest gains are for the models that resist direct requests (GPT-5 38.33→96.66%, Qwen3 51.67→100%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intent-masking paraphrase of harmful algorithm requests bypasses refusal in models that resist the direct form.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-level defenses cut direct-request ASR (SAGE D_Base mean 12.64%, Self-Reminder 29.74%). Under MOBjailbreak, ASR stays at 80.77–92.91%. SAGE raises DeepSeek-V3.1's XSTest benign refusal from 1.2% to 72%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Plug-and-play prompt defenses block direct harmful requests but not benign-paraphrased ones, and can cause over-refusal.

record.problems: MalOptBench contains 60 requests and focuses only on intelligent optimization algorithms. The reported evaluation uses an LLM-based classifier and GPT-4o harmfulness ratings; three API responses are generated, but no error bars or confidence intervals are reported. The paper notes the benchmark's modest scale. The prompt-level defense results are averaged across tasks.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was reached after recording all per-model original and MOBjailbreak ASR and harmfulness results and the aggregate D_Target/D_Joint defense results. Omitted Table 4 D_Base rows, Table 4 per-model results, and Figure 4's attention analysis; these do not test the first-response-token or KL claims. Table 4 D_Base and per-model defense details are in Section 5.2/Table 4; attention analysis is in Section 5.3/Figure 4.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models over response positions.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding attack, and no test of whether the bypass works past the opening tokens. Benign paraphrasing of the prompt is a different attack.
No weight or rank localization of safety.
No test of whether data or the objective causes shallowness. The input-attention analysis covers only prompt tokens.
No deepening or data-augmentation defense. Only prompt-level plug-and-play defenses are tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T2/V4 linkage is rejected: benign prompt paraphrasing is not one of V4's named mechanisms (prefill, suffix, decoding), and the study never examines response-opening tokens. The ASR classifier counts any non-refusal of the rewritten (benign) prompt as success, so the near-100% jailbreak ASR partly reflects that the rewritten tasks are innocuous. No variance or confidence intervals are reported. The D_Base and per-model Table 4 rows are omitted, but they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Fine-tuning on harmful examples and its effect on refusal.
Fine-tuning on ordinary or carefully chosen benign data and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models across harmful-prompt response positions.
Tests benign prompt rewriting as a jailbreak, not compliant-start prefilling, adversarial suffixes, decoding changes, or whether bypass works by getting past the first response tokens.
Whether safety behaviour is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Whether data or a training objective causes safety shallowness.
Training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens and its robustness.

rows.subject: GPT-4o
rows.operation_detail: Applied MOBjailbreak benign rewriting to MalOptBench prompts, then evaluated target responses.
rows.note: Harmfulness remains very high under rewriting.
rows.check: Linked to V4 in error, for the same reason: this is a paraphrase attack. Harmfulness falls slightly for 7 models (e.g. DeepSeek-V3 5.00→4.77, ERNIE 5.00→4.82) and is flat for Grok-3-mini, so 'observed' is not uniform. The ASR classifier only checks for non-refusal of the rewritten prompt, and GPT-4o scores harm against the original goal. The outputs (e.g. a 'logistics hub' scoring algorithm in Fig. 3) are answers to benign tasks, so harmfulness reflects how transferable the content is, not a defeat of refusal.

tranche.reason: The study tests request rewriting and algorithm-design safety, without testing or using any claim version. Its input-token importance analysis does not measure response-position alignment or explain shallowness through training.

source_check.notes: Section 4.2 uses three responses per prompt, counting success if any succeeds; harmfulness is scored on a randomly selected successful response when available. Appendix B's ASR classifier measures cooperation versus refusal, rather than independently verifying algorithm effectiveness.
